analysis.one_liner: Treats ghost-gun kits and armor-piercing concealable weapons as regulated firearms and requires police notification of denied gun checks.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 18, 2021 with 12 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to House committees and sent to a Judiciary subcommittee on November 9, 2021, and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal gun laws in three ways. It would treat do-it-yourself gun assembly kits, which currently can be sold without serial numbers or background checks, as firearms under federal law. It would add small, concealable weapons that fire rounds capable of penetrating police body armor to the National Firearms Act, the strictest tier of federal gun regulation, which requires registration and a tax. It would also write into law the existing rule that classifies bump stocks as machine guns, and it would require the Justice Department to tell state and local police within 24 hours whenever someone fails a gun background check.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun violence, since kits that become untraceable guns and concealable armor-piercing weapons would face registration requirements. Law enforcement officers gain directly: concealable weapons that can defeat standard body armor would be regulated, and police would be told within a day when a prohibited person fails a background check, allowing follow-up investigations before a gun is obtained another way.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities affected by gun violence and police

how_it_helps.text: Closes the 'ghost gun' gap by defining any combination of parts designed to convert a device into a readily assembled firearm as a firearm subject to federal regulation, so kits could no longer be sold outside background check and serial number rules.

Adds armor-piercing, concealable weapons to the National Firearms Act, requiring existing owners to register within 18 months and subjecting future sales to the registration and tax regime that already applies to machine guns and silencers.
Gives statutory force to the ATF's 2018 rule classifying bump-stock devices as machine guns, so the rule could not simply be rescinded by a future administration.

Requires the Attorney General to report denied background checks to state and local police within 24 hours, and to report annually to Congress on how many denial cases are referred, investigated, and prosecuted.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms makers and sellers of unfinished receiver kits, bump stocks, and small concealable weapons, who would face a regulated market instead of an unregulated one. Lawful current owners of the newly covered weapons would need to register them within 18 months and pay the National Firearms Act tax, and future buyers of covered items would face registration paperwork, transfer approval, and the tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun kit and accessory makers, some buyers

drawbacks.text: National Firearms Act rules impose a tax and registration process on lawful owners; people holding covered weapons at enactment would have had to register them within 18 months or become in violation, which falls on individual gun owners, not just traffickers.

The definition of an armor-piercing, concealable weapon gives ATF open-ended authority over 'any other round' it determines can penetrate standard body armor, which critics could see as granting regulators power to sweep in common calibers beyond the six listed.
Converting an agency rule into statute locks in the bump-stock classification by law, removing flexibility to revisit the rule if courts or evidence pointed the other way.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets specific, well-documented gaps: kits that become untraceable guns, small weapons firing armor-piercing rounds, and denied checks that police never hear about. The costs fall mostly on manufacturers of those products and on lawful owners of the newly covered weapons, who would face registration and the existing transfer tax. The 18-month registration window and the broad ATF authority over additional calibers are legitimate fairness and overreach concerns, but the burden on ordinary owners is limited to a narrow category of concealable, high-penetration weapons.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its crime subcommittee in November 2021, and never got a committee markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Val Demings introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, with 12 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, for its tax provisions, to the Ways and Means Committee.
On November 9, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, the last action of record.
No markup, vote, or further action occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of unserialized gun kits, bump stocks, and concealable armor-piercing weapons, who kept an unregulated market for two more years, since the restrictions never advanced.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; after its November 9, 2021 referral to the crime subcommittee, the bill took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was entirely Democratic, with 12 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.

industries.industry: Firearms makers and sellers of unfinished receiver ('ghost gun') kits
industries.note: The bill would make readily assembled gun kits 'firearms' under federal law, ending their sale outside serial number and background check rules. Today these kits reach people who could not pass a background check, so the industry's unregulated sales channel runs against public safety.

industries.industry: Bump stock and firearm accessory manufacturers
industries.note: The bill writes the 2018 ATF rule into statute, making the bump-stock-as-machine-gun classification permanent law rather than a rule a future administration could rescind.

industries.industry: Owners and dealers of concealable, armor-penetrating weapons
industries.note: These weapons would move into the National Firearms Act regime, requiring registration of existing devices within 18 months and the standard transfer process and tax for future ones.
Police would receive 24-hour notice of denied background checks and an annual accounting of enforcement, and officers would face fewer concealable weapons capable of defeating their body armor.
